lessons.title: Measurement, units and basic maths for mechanics
lessons.html:
Why measurement matters

A mechanic works with exact sizes. A bolt that is too loose can fall out. A bolt that is too tight can snap or strip the thread. A bearing with the wrong clearance will fail. You must measure correctly and use the right units.

SI units used in the workshop

WhatUnitExample
Lengthmillimetre (mm), metre (m)A 13 mm spanner
Masskilogram (kg)Weight of a wheel weight
Volumelitre (L)Engine oil capacity
Pressurekilopascal (kPa) or barTyre pressure
Torquenewton metre (N.m)Wheel nut tightness
Temperaturedegrees CelsiusCoolant temperature

Some older tractors and tools use inches and pounds. Know the difference: 1 inch is 25.4 mm. Never use an inch spanner on a metric nut because it can round the corners.

Measuring tools

  • Steel rule and tape: rough lengths.
  • Vernier caliper: outside, inside and depth to about a tenth of a millimetre or better.
  • Micrometer: very accurate outside sizes, such as shaft diameters.
  • Feeler gauges: thin blades to measure small gaps, such as valve clearance.
  • Torque wrench: tightens bolts to a set torque.

Look after measuring tools. Keep them clean, in their boxes and never drop them.

Basic maths

You will add, subtract, multiply and divide, work with decimals and fractions, and calculate percentages. Example: a tractor holds 12 L of engine oil and the dipstick shows it is 25 percent low. How much must you add? 25 percent of 12 L is 3 L. Always take values such as oil capacity and torque from the service manual, not from memory.

lessons.title: Forces, materials and how machines work
lessons.html:
Basic science for mechanics

Tractors use simple science to do heavy work. Knowing the basics helps you understand why parts fail and how to fix them.

Force, work and power

  • Force is a push or a pull, measured in newtons. A tractor pulling a plough applies force through the drawbar.
  • Torque is a turning force: force multiplied by the length of the lever. A longer spanner gives more torque with the same push.
  • Work is force moving something a distance.
  • Power is how fast work is done, measured in kilowatts (kW). Tractor engines are rated in kW, sometimes in horsepower.

Levers, gears and pulleys

A lever lets a small force move a big load. Gears and pulleys change speed and torque. A small gear driving a big gear turns the big gear slower but with more torque. This is how a tractor gearbox gives low speed and high pulling power for ploughing, and higher speed for road travel.

Friction and lubrication

Friction is the force that resists sliding. Brakes and clutches need friction to work. Bearings, gears and pistons need oil or grease to reduce friction and wear. Without lubrication, metal parts heat up, wear quickly and can seize.

Heat and pressure

Metals expand when hot and shrink when cold. This is why engine parts have clearances and why you should not open a hot radiator cap: the coolant is under pressure and can spray out and burn you. Hydraulic systems use liquid under pressure to lift heavy implements.

Materials

Tractors are made of steel, cast iron, aluminium, rubber and plastics. Steel is strong; cast iron is hard but can crack if hit or heated unevenly; aluminium is light but soft. Bolts are graded by strength, marked on the head. Always replace a bolt with one of the same grade.

Key points

  • Use SI units and the right tool, and never mix inch and metric tools.
  • Take torques and capacities from the service manual.
  • Gears trade speed for torque.
  • Lubrication reduces friction, heat and wear.
  • Never open a hot radiator cap, and replace bolts with the same grade.
